claims.question: Q1. May an OFL font be embedded in a document (PDF, SVG, web page) that is distributed under a different licence? Does the document become subject to the OFL?
claims.answer: Yes. OFL-FAQ 1.12 permits embedding in a document, in full or as a subset.
claims.verbatim_quote:
1.12  So can I embed OFL fonts in my document?
Yes, either in full or a subset. The restrictions regarding font modification and redistribution do not apply, as the font is not intended for use outside the document.

verdict.reason:
I downloaded https://openfontlicense.org/documents/OFL-FAQ.txt with curl (HTTP 200, 61,623 bytes; header "Version 1.1-update7 - November 2023") and also fetched it with WebFetch.

(a) The quote is there. Lines 60-61 read, word for word: "1.12  So can I embed OFL fonts in my document?" / "Yes, either in full or a subset. The restrictions regarding font modification and redistribution do not apply, as the font is not intended for use outside the document."

(b) The claim follows from the quote. "OFL-FAQ 1.12 permits embedding in a document, in full or as a subset" is a fair reading and adds nothing the quote does not say. So the claim is not refuted.

The claim is incomplete, though, in three ways:
1. It never answers the second half of Q1 (does the document become subject to the OFL?). Entry 1.12 says nothing about the document's own licence either, so the "under a different licence" part of the "Yes" really rests on entry 1.13, which the claim does not cite. Lines 63-64: "1.13  Does embedding alter the license of the document itself?" / "No. Referencing or embedding an OFL font in any document does not change the license of the document itself. The requirement for fonts to remain under the OFL does not apply to any document created using the fonts and their derivatives. Similarly, creating any kind of graphic using a font under the OFL does not make the resulting artwork subject to the OFL."
2. The licence itself says the same thing. Condition 5 of https://openfontlicense.org/documents/OFL.txt (HTTP 200) states that "The requirement for fonts to remain under this license does not apply to any document created using the Font Software" (lines 78-82, wrapped). A second, preamble sentence (line 30) ends "...to any document created using the fonts or their derivatives." I only grep-confirmed its end, not its full wording.
3. The FAQ does not call web pages "embedding". Entry 2.10 (line 150-151, "Isn't use of webfonts another form of embedding?") answers "No. Unlike embedded fonts in a PDF, webfonts are not an integrated part of the document itself." Entry 2.1 (line 111) says loading fonts through CSS @font-face "is recommended and explicitly allowed by the licensing model because it is distribution." So 1.12 supports PDFs and similar documents, but a web page's use of an OFL font falls under 2.1 as distribution, not under 1.12. The claim does not explicitly say 1.12 covers web pages, so this is a gap, not an error.

None of the FAQ entries cited here mentions SVG, so the SVG case is unresolved from these texts. Entry 1.11 defines embedding as "inclusion of the font in a document or file in a way that makes extraction (and redistribution) difficult or clearly discouraged", so whether a given SVG counts depends on how the font is included.

This is a report of what the texts say, not legal advice.

FAQ 3.1 ('not allowed to remove the copyright statement(s) from the font') and the paper's 'not allowed at all' rule on metadata removal are both about modified or webfont distribution, not document embedding. Whether an embedded subset may drop the copyright notice is not settled by these texts.

SVG: the FAQ uses PDF as its only example of document embedding and never mentions SVG documents. The paper's 'SVG' section is about the SVG webfont FORMAT ('conversion to SVG needs to be considered a Modified Version for which RFN restrictions apply'), not glyph outlines placed in an SVG graphic. No fetched text says whether a font subset stored inside an SVG file (e.g. an @font-face data URI) counts as document embedding (FAQ 1.12) or as a webfont (FAQ 2.x). Text converted to paths is closest to the artwork entries (FAQ 1.1.1, 1.13 'creating any kind of graphic'), but no text says so explicitly.

Web pages with a font inlined as a data URI: FAQ 2.10 and the paper say webfonts are not embedding because they are separate, reusable resources. Neither addresses a subset inlined into one HTML page, so which rule set applies there is not resolved.

RFN in embedded documents: the statement that RFNs are allowed when modification is 'only part of the embedding process - such as in a PDF' comes from the official 'Webfonts and Reserved Font Names' paper on openfontlicense.org, not from OFL-FAQ.txt itself. The FAQ text has no entry on RFNs for embedded subsets.

STIX RFN: the stipub/stixfonts OFL.txt (master and tag v2.14) declares RFN "TM Math", not "STIX". The 2021 commit history of that file includes 'Demux copyright and trademark notices' and 'Reverted AUTHORS.txt and OFL.txt'. Nothing fetched explains the choice, and the name table of the source TTF carries no RFN declaration. Whether a font actually named 'STIX Two' is affected by an RFN is not resolved from these texts.

STIX shipped binaries: the repo tree (master, v2.14) contains no built STIX Two v2.1x OTF/TTF/WOFF2, and the GitHub releases API lists no assets. So the name table was read only from source/STIXTwoText-Regular.input.ttf, a build input. The released binaries' metadata was not checked.
